name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q01 - Contrasting traits in garden pea studied by Mendel

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding contrasting traits in garden pea studied by Mendel:

List I (Character) List II (Contrasting Traits: Dominant / Recessive)
A. Pod shape I. Axial / Terminal
B. Pod colour II. Green / Yellow
C. Seed colour III. Inflated / Constricted
D. Flower position IV. Yellow / Green

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Pod Shape Evaluation
In garden pea (Pisum sativum), Mendel studied two contrasting traits for pod shape: inflated (full) pod is the dominant trait and constricted pod is the recessive trait.

Step 2: Pod Colour Evaluation
For pod colour, green pod is the dominant trait and yellow pod is the recessive trait.

Step 3: Seed Colour Evaluation
For seed colour (cotyledon colour), yellow seed is the dominant trait and green seed is the recessive trait.

Step 4: Flower Position Evaluation
For flower position, axial flower is the dominant trait and terminal flower is the recessive trait.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Matching each character to its opposing traits gives: Pod shape pairs with Inflated / Constricted (III); Pod colour pairs with Green / Yellow (II); Seed colour pairs with Yellow / Green (IV); and Flower position pairs with Axial / Terminal (I).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-III, B-II, C-IV, D-I (Pod shape: Inflated / Constricted; Pod colour: Green / Yellow; Seed colour: Yellow / Green; Flower position: Axial / Terminal).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q02 - Genetic disorders and their specific chromosomal basis

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding human genetic disorders and their causal basis:

List I (Disorder) List II (Chromosomal / Genetic Basis)
A. Down's syndrome I. Trisomy of chromosome 21
B. Turner's syndrome II. Monosomy of X chromosome (45, X0)
C. Klinefelter's syndrome III. Sex chromosome trisomy (47, XXY)
D. Sickle-cell anaemia IV. Autosome-linked recessive gene mutation

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Down's Syndrome Analysis
Down's syndrome is an autosomal aneuploidy caused by the failure of segregation of chromatids during cell division, resulting in an additional copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21).

Step 2: Turner's Syndrome Analysis
Turner's syndrome is a sex chromosome monosomy in human females resulting from the absence of one X chromosome, giving a karyotype of 45 with X0.

Step 3: Klinefelter's Syndrome Analysis
Klinefelter's syndrome is caused by the presence of an extra copy of an X chromosome in a male, resulting in a karyotype of 47, XXY.

Step 4: Sickle-Cell Anaemia Analysis
Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosome-linked recessive Mendelian disorder controlled by a pair of alleles, \(Hb^A\) and \(Hb^S\), where homozygous \(Hb^S Hb^S\) individuals exhibit the diseased condition.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Down's syndrome corresponds to Trisomy of chromosome 21 (I); Turner's syndrome corresponds to Monosomy of X chromosome (45, X0) (II); Klinefelter's syndrome corresponds to Sex chromosome trisomy (47, XXY) (III); and Sickle-cell anaemia corresponds to Autosome-linked recessive gene mutation (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (Down's syndrome: Trisomy 21; Turner's syndrome: Monosomy X0; Klinefelter's syndrome: Karyotype 47, XXY; Sickle-cell anaemia: Autosome-linked recessive mutation).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q03 - Geneticists and their key discoveries in heredity

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding key contributors and their scientific milestones in genetics:

List I (Scientist / Geneticist) List II (Contribution / Discovery)
A. Gregor Mendel I. Formulated the chromosomal theory of inheritance
B. Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri II. Proposed statistical rules of inheritance from pea hybridisation
C. Thomas Hunt Morgan III. Developed genetic maps using recombination frequencies
D. Alfred Sturtevant IV. Verified chromosomal theory experimentally and discovered linkage

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Gregor Mendel's Contribution
Gregor Mendel conducted hybridisation experiments on garden peas for seven years (1856-1863), applying statistical analysis and mathematical logic to formulate the fundamental laws of inheritance in living organisms.

Step 2: Walter Sutton and Theodore Boveri's Contribution
In 1902, Sutton and Boveri observed that chromosome behavior parallels gene behavior during meiosis and united chromosomal segregation with Mendelian principles to formulate the chromosomal theory of inheritance.

Step 3: Thomas Hunt Morgan's Contribution
Thomas Hunt Morgan used Drosophila melanogaster to provide experimental verification of the chromosomal theory of inheritance, discovering sex-linkage and coining the terms linkage and recombination.

Step 4: Alfred Sturtevant's Contribution
Alfred Sturtevant, Morgan's student, utilised the frequency of recombination between gene pairs located on the same chromosome as a quantitative measure of distance to construct the first genetic chromosome maps.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Mendel corresponds to Proposed statistical rules of inheritance from pea hybridisation (II); Sutton and Boveri correspond to Formulated the chromosomal theory of inheritance (I); Morgan corresponds to Verified chromosomal theory experimentally and discovered linkage (IV); and Sturtevant corresponds to Developed genetic maps using recombination frequencies (III).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-II, B-I, C-IV, D-III (Gregor Mendel: Statistical laws of inheritance; Sutton and Boveri: Chromosomal theory of inheritance; Thomas Hunt Morgan: Experimental verification of linkage; Alfred Sturtevant: Genetic mapping).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q04 - Mechanisms of sex determination across different organisms

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding mechanisms of sex determination in different organisms:

List I (Organism) List II (Sex Determining Mechanism)
A. Grasshopper I. Female heterogamety (ZW females and ZZ males)
B. Birds II. Male heterogamety with XO type
C. Drosophila III. Male heterogamety with XY type
D. Honey bee IV. Haplodiploid system

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Grasshopper Sex Determination
In grasshoppers, sex determination is of the XO type (male heterogamety), where females have a pair of X chromosomes (XX) and males possess only a single X chromosome (XO) besides autosomes.

Step 2: Birds Sex Determination
In birds, sex determination operates via female heterogamety; females produce two morphologically distinct sex chromosomes designated Z and W (ZW), while males have two identical Z chromosomes (ZZ).

Step 3: Drosophila Sex Determination
In Drosophila melanogaster (as well as humans), sex determination is of the XY type (male heterogamety), where females have an XX chromosomal pair and males carry an XY pair along with autosomes.

Step 4: Honey Bee Sex Determination
In honey bees, sex is governed by a haplodiploid system: females (queens or workers) develop from fertilised eggs and are diploid (\(2n = 32\)), while males (drones) develop parthenogenetically from unfertilised eggs and are haploid (\(n = 16\)).

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Grasshopper corresponds to Male heterogamety with XO type (II); Birds correspond to Female heterogamety (ZW females and ZZ males) (I); Drosophila corresponds to Male heterogamety with XY type (III); and Honey bee corresponds to Haplodiploid system (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-II, B-I, C-III, D-IV (Grasshopper: XO male heterogamety; Birds: ZW female heterogamety; Drosophila: XY male heterogamety; Honey bee: Haplodiploidy).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q05 - Patterns of non Mendelian inheritance and examples

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding non-Mendelian genetic phenomena and their representative biological examples:

List I (Phenomenon) List II (Representative Example / Feature)
A. Incomplete dominance I. Pink flower colour in Antirrhinum majus
B. Co-dominance II. Simultaneous expression of \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) sugar polymers in RBCs
C. Pleiotropy III. Phenylketonuria leading to mental retardation and pigment reduction
D. Polygenic inheritance IV. Additive phenotypic gradient of human skin colour

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Incomplete Dominance Analysis
In incomplete dominance, the heterozygous phenotype is an intermediate blending between the two parental types. A classic example is flower colour in Snapdragon (Antirrhinum sp.), where crossing red (RR) with white (rr) yields pink (Rr) \(F_1\) flowers.

Step 2: Co-Dominance Analysis
In co-dominance, both alleles express their specific products completely and independently in the heterozygote. In the human ABO blood group system, the \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) alleles present together produce both A-type and B-type sugar polymers on the surface of erythrocytes.

Step 3: Pleiotropy Analysis
Pleiotropy occurs when a single gene mutation influences multiple distinct phenotypic traits. In phenylketonuria, a single gene mutation abolishing phenylalanine hydroxylase manifests as both severe mental retardation and diminished hair and skin pigmentation.

Step 4: Polygenic Inheritance Analysis
Polygenic inheritance refers to traits controlled by three or more genes exhibiting a continuous phenotypic gradient with an additive allele effect and environmental influence, as exemplified by human skin pigmentation.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Incomplete dominance pairs with Pink flower colour in Antirrhinum majus (I); Co-dominance pairs with Simultaneous expression of \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) sugar polymers in RBCs (II); Pleiotropy pairs with Phenylketonuria leading to mental retardation and pigment reduction (III); and Polygenic inheritance pairs with Additive phenotypic gradient of human skin colour (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (Incomplete dominance: Snapdragon flower colour; Co-dominance: ABO blood group \(I^A I^B\); Pleiotropy: Phenylketonuria multiple symptoms; Polygenic inheritance: Human skin colour).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q06 - Genetic disorders and their distinguishing clinical features

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding human genetic disorders and their characteristic diagnostic clinical features:

List I (Disorder) List II (Characteristic Clinical Manifestation)
A. Down's syndrome I. Overall masculine development with gynaecomastia and sterility
B. Klinefelter's syndrome II. Short statured sterile female with rudimentary ovaries
C. Turner's syndrome III. Mental retardation due to accumulation of phenylpyruvic acid
D. Phenylketonuria IV. Furrowed tongue, broad flat face, and palm crease

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Down's Syndrome Clinical Features
An individual affected with Down's syndrome is short statured with a small round head, furrowed tongue, partially open mouth, broad face, characteristic palm crease, and retarded physical, psychomotor, and mental development.

Step 2: Klinefelter's Syndrome Clinical Features
An individual with Klinefelter's syndrome (47, XXY) exhibits overall masculine development along with feminine development such as breast development (gynaecomastia) and is sterile.

Step 3: Turner's Syndrome Clinical Features
A female with Turner's syndrome (45, X0) is sterile due to rudimentary ovaries, displays short stature, and lacks normal secondary sexual characteristics.

Step 4: Phenylketonuria Clinical Features
In phenylketonuria, lack of phenylalanine hydroxylase leads to accumulation of phenylalanine and its conversion to phenylpyruvic acid and derivatives, which accumulate in the brain causing severe mental retardation and are excreted in urine due to poor kidney reabsorption.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Down's syndrome corresponds to Furrowed tongue, broad flat face, and palm crease (IV); Klinefelter's syndrome corresponds to Overall masculine development with gynaecomastia and sterility (I); Turner's syndrome corresponds to Short statured sterile female with rudimentary ovaries (II); and Phenylketonuria corresponds to Mental retardation due to accumulation of phenylpyruvic acid (III).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-IV, B-I, C-II, D-III (Down's syndrome: Furrowed tongue and palm crease; Klinefelter's syndrome: Gynaecomastia in sterile male; Turner's syndrome: Rudimentary ovaries in sterile female; Phenylketonuria: Brain damage and urinary phenylpyruvate).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q07 - ABO blood group genotypes and their phenotypes

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding human ABO blood group genotypes and their expressed phenotypes:

List I (Genotype) List II (Expressed Blood Group Phenotype)
A. \(I^A I^B\) I. Blood group AB
B. \(I^A i\) II. Blood group A
C. \(I^B I^B\) III. Blood group B
D. \(i i\) IV. Blood group O

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Genotype \(I^A I^B\) Analysis
The alleles \(I^A\) and \(I^B\) are co-dominant to each other; when both alleles are present in the genotype \(I^A I^B\), both produce their respective surface sugars, resulting in blood group AB.

Step 2: Genotype \(I^A i\) Analysis
The allele \(I^A\) is completely dominant over the recessive allele \(i\), which produces no sugar polymer. Therefore, the heterozygous genotype \(I^A i\) expresses blood group A.

Step 3: Genotype \(I^B I^B\) Analysis
The homozygous genotype \(I^B I^B\) carries two copies of the \(I^B\) allele, synthesizing B-type sugar polymers and yielding blood group B.

Step 4: Genotype \(i i\) Analysis
The homozygous recessive genotype \(i i\) lacks functional transferase enzymes to synthesize either A or B surface sugars, resulting in blood group O.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
\(I^A I^B\) matches Blood group AB (I); \(I^A i\) matches Blood group A (II); \(I^B I^B\) matches Blood group B (III); and \(i i\) matches Blood group O (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (\(I^A I^B\): Blood group AB; \(I^A i\): Blood group A; \(I^B I^B\): Blood group B; \(i i\): Blood group O).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q08 - Mendelian blood disorders and their underlying causes

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding hereditary blood disorders and their precise genetic or molecular mechanisms:

List I (Blood Disorder) List II (Underlying Genetic / Molecular Cause)
A. \(\alpha\)-Thalassemia I. Controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16
B. \(\beta\)-Thalassemia II. Controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11
C. Sickle-cell anaemia III. Transversion of GAG to GUG at the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin chain
D. Haemophilia IV. X-linked recessive defect in a clotting cascade protein

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: \(\alpha\)-Thalassemia Mechanism
\(\alpha\)-Thalassemia is an autosome-linked recessive blood disorder controlled by two tightly linked genes, HBA1 and HBA2, situated on chromosome 16 of each parent, resulting from deletion or mutation of one or more of these four genes.

Step 2: \(\beta\)-Thalassemia Mechanism
\(\beta\)-Thalassemia is an autosomal recessive condition controlled by a single gene, HBB, situated on chromosome 11 of each parent, caused by mutation of one or both alleles leading to reduced synthesis of \(\beta\)-globin chains.

Step 3: Sickle-Cell Anaemia Mechanism
Sickle-cell anaemia is an autosomal recessive qualitative disorder caused by a single point mutation (base substitution) converting codon GAG to GUG at the sixth position of the \(\beta\)-globin gene, replacing glutamic acid (Glu) with valine (Val).

Step 4: Haemophilia Mechanism
Haemophilia is a sex-linked recessive disorder where a single protein involved in the cascade of blood clotting is defective, transmitted from unaffected heterozygous carrier females to male progeny.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
\(\alpha\)-Thalassemia pairs with Controlled by two closely linked genes HBA1 and HBA2 on chromosome 16 (I); \(\beta\)-Thalassemia pairs with Controlled by a single gene HBB on chromosome 11 (II); Sickle-cell anaemia pairs with Transversion of GAG to GUG at the sixth codon of the \(\beta\)-globin chain (III); and Haemophilia pairs with X-linked recessive defect in a clotting cascade protein (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (\(\alpha\)-Thalassemia: HBA1/HBA2 on chromosome 16; \(\beta\)-Thalassemia: HBB on chromosome 11; Sickle-cell anaemia: Sixth codon GAG to GUG substitution; Haemophilia: X-linked clotting protein defect).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q09 - Recombination frequencies and crosses in Drosophila genetics

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding classical genetic crosses and their characteristic quantitative outcomes:

List I (Cross / Genetic Setup) List II (Quantitative Outcome / Frequency)
A. Morgan's Cross A (yellow body \(y\) and white eye \(w\)) I. 1.3 per cent recombinant progeny
B. Morgan's Cross B (white eye \(w\) and miniature wing \(m\)) II. 37.2 per cent recombinant progeny
C. Mendel's dihybrid cross \(F_2\) generation III. 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio
D. Typical monohybrid test cross IV. 1:1 phenotypic ratio

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Morgan's Cross A Frequency Analysis
In Morgan's dihybrid cross in Drosophila between yellow body and white eye genes located on the X chromosome, the genes were tightly linked, yielding 98.7 per cent parental types and only 1.3 per cent recombinants.

Step 2: Morgan's Cross B Frequency Analysis
In Morgan's cross between white eye and miniature wing genes on the X chromosome, the genes were loosely linked, exhibiting a higher recombination frequency of 37.2 per cent (with 62.8 per cent parental types).

Step 3: Mendelian Dihybrid \(F_2\) Ratio Analysis
In a standard Mendelian dihybrid cross involving two independently assorting unlinked genes, selfing of the heterozygous \(F_1\) (\(RrYy\)) yields a phenotypic ratio of 9:3:3:1 in the \(F_2\) generation.

Step 4: Monohybrid Test Cross Ratio Analysis
In a typical monohybrid test cross, a heterozygous individual showing the dominant phenotype (\(Tt\)) is crossed with a homozygous recessive parent (\(tt\)), producing dominant and recessive phenotypes in a 1:1 ratio.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Morgan's Cross A corresponds to 1.3 per cent recombinant progeny (I); Morgan's Cross B corresponds to 37.2 per cent recombinant progeny (II); Mendel's dihybrid \(F_2\) corresponds to 9:3:3:1 phenotypic ratio (III); and Monohybrid test cross corresponds to 1:1 phenotypic ratio (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (Cross A: 1.3% recombinants; Cross B: 37.2% recombinants; Dihybrid \(F_2\): 9:3:3:1 ratio; Monohybrid test cross: 1:1 ratio).

name.text: NEET_UG_BIOLOGY_PRINCIPLES_OF_INHERITANCE_AND_VARIATION_MATCHING_MCQ_Q10 - Pedigree analysis symbols and their specific meanings

questiontext.text:
Match List I with List II regarding standard symbols used in human pedigree analysis:

List I (Pedigree Symbol) List II (Standard Significance)
A. Double horizontal line connecting male and female I. Consanguineous mating (mating between relatives)
B. Fully shaded square or circle II. Affected individual
C. Diamond with numeral 5 inscribed III. Five unaffected offspring
D. Unshaded diamond IV. Sex unspecified

Choose the correct answer from the options given below:

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Consanguineous Mating Symbol Interpretation
In human pedigree analysis, a single horizontal line connecting a square and a circle represents standard mating, whereas a double horizontal line between them signifies consanguineous mating (mating between close relatives).

Step 2: Affected Individual Symbol Interpretation
Standard pedigree charts represent unaffected individuals with open (unshaded) geometric shapes, whereas individuals affected by the genetic trait or disorder are represented by solid, fully shaded symbols.

Step 3: Inscribed Diamond Symbol Interpretation
When multiple unaffected siblings of unspecified gender are to be represented compactly, a diamond containing an Arabic numeral is used; therefore, a diamond containing the number 5 represents five unaffected offspring.

Step 4: Unshaded Diamond Interpretation
A square denotes a male and a circle denotes a female; an unshaded diamond symbol is used when the sex of the individual is unspecified.

Step 5: Synthesis of Pairings
Double horizontal line connecting male and female corresponds to Consanguineous mating (mating between relatives) (I); Fully shaded square or circle corresponds to Affected individual (II); Diamond with numeral 5 inscribed corresponds to Five unaffected offspring (III); and Unshaded diamond corresponds to Sex unspecified (IV).

Final Answer:
The correct matching combination is A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV (Double line: Consanguineous mating; Shaded shape: Affected individual; Diamond with 5: Five unaffected offspring; Diamond: Sex unspecified).
